questions.question: The forward reaction in the equilibrium $\text{OCl}^{-}$(aq) + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l) ⇌ $\text{HOCl}$(aq) + $\text{OH}^{-}$(aq) is endothermic. Which change increases the concentration of the hypochlorous acid ($\text{HOCl}$)?
questions.answer: Adding $\text{NaOCl}$ increases $\text{OCl}^{-}$, so the equilibrium shifts right (Le Chatelier) and $\text{HOCl}$ increases (B). Water is a liquid, so adding it does not change the position; adding $\text{OH}^{-}$ shifts the equilibrium left; lowering the temperature shifts it left (the forward reaction is endothermic).

questions.question: 0.1 moles of each of the following substances is dissolved in 1 L of water. For which substance would the pH of the solution be the closest to 14?
questions.answer: $\text{Ca(OH)}_{2}$ is a strong base giving two $\text{OH}^{-}$ per formula unit, so $[\text{OH}^-]$ = 0.2 M, pOH = 0.70 and pH ≈ 13.3 (A). Ethanol is neutral, $\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl}$ is acidic and $\text{NaCH}_{3}\text{COO}$ is only weakly basic.

questions.question: A saturated solution of $\text{BaSO}_{4}$ is maintained at constant temperature. Solid soluble $\text{Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ is added to this solution. What happens to the $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ ion concentrations in the resultant solution compared to the initial solution?
questions.answer: Common ion effect: $\text{Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ dissolves completely and raises $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]$, so the equilibrium $\text{BaSO}_{4}$(s) ⇌ $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ + $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ shifts left. Some $\text{BaSO}_{4}$ precipitates, so $[\text{Ba}^{2+}]$ falls, but the total $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]$ ends higher than before, because $K_{sp}$ is constant (C).
options: $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ concentration increases and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ concentration remains the same
$\text{Ba}^{2+}$ concentration decreases and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ concentration remains the same

questions.question: The graph shows the changes in pH during a titration. Which indicator should be chosen for this titration?
questions.answer: The pH starts at about 14 (a strong base in the flask) and falls steeply between about pH 12 and pH 6, to a weakly acidic final pH of about 5. The indicator's range must lie within the steep section: phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0) changes colour entirely within it (D). Methyl orange and bromocresol green change below the vertical section and would give a gradual, unclear end-point.

questions.question: Which of these substances is an example of a polyprotic acid?
questions.answer: A polyprotic acid can donate more than one proton per molecule. $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HNO}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ each donate one proton (monoprotic). Only the option with three ionisable hydrogen atoms, $\text{H}_{3}\text{CrO}_{4}$, is polyprotic (C).

questions.question: Below is an equation for a reversible reaction: 2$\text{CrO}_{4}^{2-}$(aq) + 2$\text{H}^{+}$(aq) ⇌ $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$(aq) + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l). The reaction's correct equilibrium expression is:
questions.answer: $K=\dfrac{[\text{products}]}{[\text{reactants}]}$ with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. Pure liquid water is omitted (its concentration is constant). So $K=\dfrac{[\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}]}{[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}]^2[\text{H}^+]^2}$ (B).

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the following compound? The six-carbon chain CH3-CH2-CHCl-CHCl-CHF-CH3 has chlorine atoms on the third and fourth carbons from the left, and a fluorine on the fifth carbon from the left (that is, the carbon next to the end carbon on the right).
questions.answer: Number the chain so that the substituents have the lowest set of locants: from the right they are at 2, 3, 4 (from the left they would be 3, 4, 5). Substituents are listed alphabetically (chloro before fluoro) with the multiplier 'di' for the two chlorines: 3,4-dichloro-2-fluorohexane (D).

questions.question: Chlorine gas ($\text{Cl}_{2}$) and carbon monoxide gas (CO) are placed in a sealed container and kept at a temperature of 25 °C. Phosgene gas is produced as follows: $\text{Cl}_{2}$(g) + CO(g) ⇌ $\text{COCl}_{2}$(g). Which statements about this reaction are correct?
questions.answer: In a closed system the reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium: the forward and reverse rates become equal, so the concentrations (including $\text{COCl}_{2}$) stop changing (D). A is wrong because the reaction is reversible and does not go to completion. C is wrong because the forward reaction does not stop at equilibrium; it continues, balanced by the reverse reaction.
options: All the $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and CO will be converted into $\text{COCl}_{2}$
At a temperature of 25 °C the $\text{COCl}_{2}$ will not form
The forward reaction will continue to occur until the concentration of $\text{COCl}_{2}$ remains constant
When the forward and reverse reactions become equal the concentration of $\text{COCl}_{2}$ becomes constant

questions.question: The molar masses of $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}$, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{F}$ are similar. Which of the following lists these compounds in order of increasing boiling point?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}$ is non-polar (dispersion forces only), so it has the lowest boiling point. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{F}$ is polar (dipole–dipole forces) and cannot hydrogen bond. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ has an O–H group and forms hydrogen bonds, the strongest of the three, so it has the highest boiling point (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows molecules P and Q reacting to form R and water. P is HCOOH (methanoic acid), Q is CH3NH2 and R is HCONHCH3. Which row of the table correctly identifies the molecule types?
questions.answer: P has a –COOH group (carboxylic acid), Q has an –NH₂ group on an alkyl group (a primary amine), and R has the –CONH– linkage (an amide), formed by a condensation reaction releasing water (A).
options: P: carboxylic acid; Q: amine; R: amide
P: carboxylic acid; Q: amide; R: amine
P: alcohol; Q: amine; R: ester
P: aldehyde; Q: amide; R: ketone

questions.question: The spectrum of visible light, structural formula and UV absorption spectrum of methylbenzene is shown. Based on the information, which statement about methylbenzene is correct?
questions.answer: The absorbance spectrum peaks at about 290 nm and is almost zero above about 350 nm, so methylbenzene absorbs in the ultraviolet and does not absorb any visible light (400–700 nm). All visible wavelengths are transmitted, so a solution appears colourless (A). The spectrum starts at 200 nm, so it says nothing about wavelengths below 100 nm.
options: A solution of methylbenzene would appear colourless
A solution of methylbenzene would appear as an orange-red colour
Methylbenzene only absorbs in the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum
Methylbenzene does not absorb wavelengths lower than 100 nm

questions.question: The graph refers to the gaseous reaction aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g). The effect of increasing pressure and temperature on the equilibrium yield of products is shown in the graph. Which of the following alternatives regarding the equilibrium systems is consistent with the data?
questions.answer: The yield of product increases as the pressure increases, so the forward reaction reduces the number of moles of gas: a + b > c + d. The yield decreases as the temperature increases (the 350 °C curve is the highest), so the forward reaction is exothermic, ΔH < 0 (C).
options: a + b < c + d, ΔH negative
a + b < c + d, ΔH positive
a + b > c + d, ΔH negative
a + b > c + d, ΔH positive

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of compounds will form a precipitate when 0.1 mol L⁻¹ solutions of each are mixed?
questions.answer: All nitrates are soluble, and so are all potassium, sodium and bromide salts of these metals, so A, B (copper(II) sulfate is soluble) and C produce no precipitate. In D, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ form insoluble copper(II) hydroxide: $\text{Cu}^{2+}$(aq) + 2$\text{OH}^{-}$(aq) → $\text{Cu(OH)}_{2}$(s) (D).

questions.question: A student performed a titration to determine the concentration of an unknown sodium hydroxide solution using a standard solution of hydrochloric acid. They performed the following steps: a burette was rinsed with deionised water, then rinsed again with the sodium hydroxide solution; the burette was then filled with the sodium hydroxide solution; a volumetric pipette and a conical flask were both washed with deionised water, then washed again with the hydrochloric acid solution; 25 mL of the hydrochloric acid solution was transferred into the conical flask using the pipette and an appropriate indicator added; the titration was performed until the end-point, and the titrant volume recorded. The calculated concentration based on the method described above will be:
questions.answer: Rinsing the burette with NaOH and the pipette with HCl is correct. Rinsing the conical flask with HCl is not: the residual acid adds extra moles of HCl to the 25 mL taken, so more NaOH is needed to reach the end-point and the titre is larger than it should be. The calculated concentration ($c_{\text{NaOH}}$ = n(HCl)/titre, using only the 25 mL pipetted) is therefore lower than the true value (B).
options: The same as the true value
Different than the true value, but there is insufficient information to determine if it would be higher or lower

questions.question: Four organic compounds are identified by the numbers I, II, III, IV: I – $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$; II – $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$; III – $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$; IV – $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. Which alternative identifies the strongest acid and strongest base in the list?
questions.answer: The carboxylic acid (I) is by far the strongest acid of the four (ethanol and the amide are neutral, the amine is basic). The amine (IV) has a lone pair on nitrogen that readily accepts a proton, while in the amide (III) the lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl group and the amide is essentially neutral. So the strongest acid is I and the strongest base is IV (B).
options: Strongest acid I, strongest base III
Strongest acid I, strongest base IV
Strongest acid II, strongest base III
Strongest acid II, strongest base IV

questions.question: The diagram shows a polymer (a carbon chain with a –CONH₂ group on every second carbon). Identify the type of polymerisation reaction used to produce it and the monomer or monomer units used to make it.
questions.answer: The backbone consists only of carbon–carbon single bonds, with a –CONH₂ side group on every second carbon, and no small molecule is lost. This is an addition polymer made from the alkene monomer CH₂=CH–CONH₂ (prop-2-enamide, acrylamide) (A). The side groups are single, not alternating with –CH₃ groups, so B is wrong, and a condensation polymer would contain linkages such as amide bonds in the backbone.
options: Condensation, from ethene and carbamic acid, H2N–COOH (two monomers)
Condensation, from two molecules of carbamic acid, H2N–COOH

questions.question: What is the function of the hollow cathode lamp in an atomic absorption spectrometer?
questions.answer: The cathode of the lamp is made of the element being analysed, so the lamp emits the characteristic wavelengths of that element. These are absorbed by the free gaseous atoms of that element in the flame (A). The flame, not the lamp, atomises the sample.
options: Provide a specific wavelength of light that can be absorbed by free atoms in the gaseous state
Separate molecules in the tested sample so that free atoms are formed
Convert free atoms in the tested sample into gaseous ions
Produce a frequency of light that is absorbed by particular bonds of molecules in the sample being tested

questions.question: The graph shows the concentrations over time for the equilibrium system 2$\text{NO}_{2}$(g) ⇌ $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$(g), ΔH = −58 kJ mol⁻¹. What has happened to the temperature at T₁ and to the volume at T₂?
questions.answer: At T₁ the concentrations change gradually (no sudden jump), so the change is a temperature change. $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ decreases and $\text{NO}_{2}$ increases, so the equilibrium shifts left, favouring the endothermic reverse reaction: the temperature increased. At T₂ both concentrations drop suddenly, so the volume increased (concentrations fall). Then $\text{NO}_{2}$ rises and $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ falls, a shift to the side with more moles of gas (2 mol of $\text{NO}_{2}$ against 1 mol of $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$), consistent with a decrease in pressure (D).
options: Temperature decreased at T₁ and volume increased at T₂
Temperature increased at T₁ and volume decreased at T₂
Temperature decreased at T₁ and volume decreased at T₂
Temperature increased at T₁ and volume increased at T₂

questions.question: A researcher was examining a sample of the polymer polyvinyl chloride (PVC) to determine its chain length. The sample was found to have a molar mass of 623 800 g mol⁻¹. A section of the chain is shown (the repeating unit –CH₂–CHCl–). What is the value of n?

1.23 g of a pure acid, $\text{H}_{2}\text{X}$(s), is added to exactly 250.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH(aq): $\text{H}_{2}\text{X}$(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → $\text{Na}_{2}\text{X}$(aq) + 2$\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l). The NaOH is in excess. This excess NaOH requires 27.50 mL of 0.20 M HCl(aq) for neutralisation. What is the molar mass of the acid?
questions.answer: n(NaOH) added $=0.100\times0.2500=0.02500$ mol. n(excess NaOH) $=n(\text{HCl})=0.20\times0.02750=0.00550$ mol. n(NaOH) reacted $=0.01950$ mol. n($\text{H}_2\text{X}$) $=\tfrac12(0.01950)=0.00975$ mol. $M=\dfrac{1.23}{0.00975}=126$ g mol⁻¹ (D).

questions.question: Students modelled chemical equilibrium using the following physical system: (1) place two beakers side by side and label them A and B; (2) add 200 M&Ms to beaker A; (3) record the number of M&Ms in each beaker; (4) transfer 20% of the M&Ms in beaker A to beaker B; (5) transfer 10% of the M&Ms in beaker B to beaker A; (6) repeat steps 3–5 until there is no more change in the number of M&Ms. Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of this procedure as a model for chemical equilibrium.
questions.answer: Strengths: (i) it shows that equilibrium is reached when the numbers stop changing, even though the transfers continue in both directions, modelling the dynamic nature of equilibrium (forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates); (ii) the transfers in the two directions are reversible, like a reversible reaction in a closed system (no M&Ms are lost); (iii) the amounts in the two beakers are not equal at equilibrium (here beaker B ends with about twice as many as A, 133 to 67), showing that equilibrium does not mean equal amounts; (iv) the same position would be reached whichever beaker started with the M&Ms. Weaknesses: (i) the transfers happen in separate, discrete steps, one after the other, whereas in a chemical system forward and reverse reactions occur simultaneously and continuously; (ii) M&Ms are not converted into a different substance, so there is no chemical change or bond breaking and forming; (iii) the fixed percentages mean the 'rate' depends only on the number in the beaker, and there is no model of collisions, energy or particle behaviour; (iv) M&Ms are macroscopic and can be counted exactly, unlike molecules, and the model cannot show the effect of temperature, pressure or concentration changes.

questions.question: Students modelled chemical equilibrium by repeatedly transferring 20% of the M&Ms in beaker A to beaker B and 10% of the M&Ms in beaker B to beaker A. Describe a change to this procedure that would model how equilibrium is affected by catalysis.
questions.answer: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally and does not change the equilibrium position. To model this, increase both transfer percentages by the same factor, e.g. transfer 40% from A to B and 20% from B to A. The same final distribution (about 67 in A and 133 in B) is reached in fewer repetitions.

questions.question: Sulfur dioxide and oxygen can be reacted to form sulfur trioxide according to the equation 2$\text{SO}_{2}$(g) + $\text{O}_{2}$(g) ⇌ 2$\text{SO}_{3}$(g). Use Le Chatelier's Principle to predict any changes in the equilibrium position if the volume of the reaction vessel is increased. Justify your response.
questions.answer: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to partially counteract the change. Increasing the volume decreases the pressure (and the concentration of all the gases). The system will shift to increase the pressure again, favouring the side with the greater number of moles of gas. The reactants have 3 mol of gas (2$\text{SO}_{2}$ + $\text{O}_{2}$) and the product has 2 mol, so the equilibrium shifts to the left (the reverse reaction is favoured), decreasing the yield of $\text{SO}_{3}$.

questions.question: Sulfur dioxide and oxygen react according to 2$\text{SO}_{2}$(g) + $\text{O}_{2}$(g) ⇌ 2$\text{SO}_{3}$(g). The volume of the reaction vessel is increased. Explain the change in the equilibrium position using collision theory.
questions.answer: Collision theory: reactions occur when particles collide with sufficient energy (at least the activation energy) and the correct orientation, so the rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions. Increasing the volume decreases the concentration of every gas, so there are fewer collisions per unit time and both the forward and reverse rates decrease. The forward reaction involves a collision of three particles (2$\text{SO}_{2}$ + $\text{O}_{2}$) and its rate depends on a higher power of concentration than the reverse reaction (two $\text{SO}_{3}$), so its rate decreases by more than that of the reverse reaction. The reverse rate is then temporarily greater than the forward rate, and the net reaction proceeds to the left until the rates are equal again at a new equilibrium with more $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $\text{O}_{2}$.

questions.question: Hydrogen and carbon monoxide react as gases as follows: 2$\text{H}_{2}$(g) + CO(g) ⇌ $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$(g). Write the equilibrium expression for this reaction.
questions.answer: $K=\dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}{[\text{H}_2]^2[\text{CO}]}$

questions.question: Hydrogen and carbon monoxide react as gases: 2$\text{H}_{2}$(g) + CO(g) ⇌ $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$(g). This reaction is exothermic. State one way that the equilibrium constant for this reaction could be increased and justify your choice.
questions.answer: Decrease the temperature. The equilibrium constant depends only on temperature (changes in concentration, pressure or the addition of a catalyst do not change it). The forward reaction is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle a decrease in temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (the system produces heat to oppose the decrease), increasing the concentration of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ and decreasing those of the reactants, so the value of K increases. (The question as printed does not state that the reaction is exothermic; the formation of methanol from CO and $\text{H}_{2}$ is exothermic.)

questions.question: 1.0 mol of $\text{H}_{2}$ and 1.0 mol of CO were placed into a 4.0 L container at 298 K, where 2$\text{H}_{2}$(g) + CO(g) ⇌ $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$(g). When the system had reached equilibrium, it was found that 0.2 mol of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ had been formed. Calculate the equilibrium constant for the reaction under these conditions.
questions.answer: Initial concentrations: $[\text{H}_2]=[\text{CO}]=\dfrac{1.0}{4.0}=0.25$ M. $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]=\dfrac{0.2}{4.0}=0.05$ M at equilibrium. Using the 1:2:1 ratios, $\text{H}_2$ decreases by 0.10 M and CO by 0.05 M. Equilibrium: $[\text{H}_2]=0.15$ M, $[\text{CO}]=0.20$ M, $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]=0.05$ M. $K=\dfrac{0.05}{(0.15)^2(0.20)}=11.1$ (about 11).

questions.question: A 10 L vessel contains 2.5 mol of $\text{H}_{2}$, 4.0 mol of CO and 3.0 mol of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ at 298 K, where 2$\text{H}_{2}$(g) + CO(g) ⇌ $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$(g) has K = 11.1 at this temperature. Is this system at equilibrium, and if not, which direction will the reaction shift to achieve equilibrium?
questions.answer: Concentrations: $[\text{H}_2]=0.25$ M, $[\text{CO}]=0.40$ M, $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]=0.30$ M. $Q=\dfrac{0.30}{(0.25)^2(0.40)}=12$. Since $Q\ne K$ (12 > 11.1), the system is not at equilibrium. There is too much product, so the reaction shifts to the left (towards the reactants) until $Q=K$.

questions.question: $K_w$ (the ionisation constant of water) is $5.50\times10^{-13}$ at 375 K. Calculate the pH of water at this temperature.
questions.answer: In pure water $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=[\text{OH}^-]$, so $K_w=[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]^2$ and $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=\sqrt{5.50\times10^{-13}}=7.42\times10^{-7}$ M. $\text{pH}=-\log(7.42\times10^{-7})=6.13$.

questions.question: $K_w$ is $5.50\times10^{-13}$ at 375 K (compared with $1.0\times10^{-14}$ at 298 K). Deduce whether the auto-ionisation of water is an exothermic or endothermic process. Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Endothermic. $K_w$ is the equilibrium constant for $2\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^++\text{OH}^-$. It increases from $1.0\times10^{-14}$ at 298 K to $5.5\times10^{-13}$ at 375 K, meaning that more products are present at equilibrium at the higher temperature. By Le Chatelier's principle an increase in temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction (ionisation) must be endothermic.

questions.question: Elemental sulfur can be used to control powdery mildew on grapes. 100.0 g of grapes were treated with 100.0 mL of surfactant solution to remove the sulfur remaining on the grapes. 25.00 mL of this surfactant solution was treated to convert all of the sulfur to sulfate ions and then dried to produce an ash containing the sulfate ions. This ash was transferred to a 10.00 mL volumetric flask containing 2.00 mL of 200 mg/L solution of barium ions. The volume was then made up to the calibration line. A precipitate of BaSO₄ formed. A small amount of the solution containing the unreacted Ba²⁺ ions was analysed using atomic absorption spectroscopy and gave an absorbance of 0.11. A calibration curve (shown) was prepared using standard solutions of 10, 20, 30 and 40 mg/L Ba²⁺(aq). Determine the mass of barium ions, in mg, remaining in the 10.00 mL sample solution.
questions.answer: From the calibration curve, an absorbance of 0.11 corresponds to $[\text{Ba}^{2+}]=19$ mg L⁻¹. Mass of $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ in 10.00 mL $=\dfrac{19}{1000}\times10.00=0.19$ mg.

questions.question: Elemental sulfur can be used to control powdery mildew on grapes. 100.0 g of grapes were treated with 100.0 mL of surfactant solution to remove the sulfur remaining on the grapes. 25.00 mL of this surfactant solution was treated to convert all of the sulfur to sulfate ions and then dried to produce an ash containing the sulfate ions. This ash was transferred to a 10.00 mL volumetric flask containing 2.00 mL of 200 mg/L solution of barium ions. The volume was then made up to the calibration line. A precipitate of BaSO₄ formed. A small amount of the solution containing the unreacted Ba²⁺ ions was analysed using atomic absorption spectroscopy and gave an absorbance of 0.11. A calibration curve (shown) was prepared using standard solutions of 10, 20, 30 and 40 mg/L Ba²⁺(aq). Determine the amount of barium ions, in moles, that reacted to produce the barium sulfate precipitate.
questions.answer: Mass of $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ added $=\dfrac{2.00}{1000}\times200=0.400$ mg. Mass remaining $=0.19$ mg. Mass reacted $=0.400-0.19=0.21$ mg $=2.1\times10^{-4}$ g. $n=\dfrac{2.1\times10^{-4}}{137.3}=1.5\times10^{-6}$ mol.

questions.question: Elemental sulfur can be used to control powdery mildew on grapes. 100.0 g of grapes were treated with 100.0 mL of surfactant solution to remove the sulfur remaining on the grapes. 25.00 mL of this surfactant solution was treated to convert all of the sulfur to sulfate ions and then dried to produce an ash containing the sulfate ions. This ash was transferred to a 10.00 mL volumetric flask containing 2.00 mL of 200 mg/L solution of barium ions. The volume was then made up to the calibration line. A precipitate of BaSO₄ formed. A small amount of the solution containing the unreacted Ba²⁺ ions was analysed using atomic absorption spectroscopy and gave an absorbance of 0.11. A calibration curve (shown) was prepared using standard solutions of 10, 20, 30 and 40 mg/L Ba²⁺(aq). Calculate the mass of sulfur, in mg, remaining on the 100.0 g of harvested grapes.
questions.answer: $\text{Ba}^{2+}+\text{SO}_4^{2-}\to\text{BaSO}_4$ (1:1), so n(sulfate) = n(S) in the 25.00 mL of surfactant solution $=1.5\times10^{-6}$ mol. The 25.00 mL is one quarter of the 100.0 mL used to wash the grapes, so n(S) on the grapes $=4\times1.5\times10^{-6}=6.0\times10^{-6}$ mol. $m(\text{S})=6.0\times10^{-6}\times32.1=1.9\times10^{-4}$ g $=0.19$ mg.

questions.question: The amount of sulfur remaining on the grapes can also be determined using gravimetric analysis. Explain two reasons why atomic absorption spectroscopy is a better way to determine the residual sulfur on the grapes, compared to gravimetric analysis.
questions.answer: (1) AAS is very sensitive and can measure very low concentrations (here mg L⁻¹), whereas gravimetric analysis is inaccurate for very small quantities: the precipitate formed would be only about 0.5 mg, and the percentage error from losses during precipitation, filtering, washing, drying and weighing would be large. (2) AAS needs only a small sample (a small volume of solution), so the measurement is quick and uses a small representative sample, whereas gravimetric analysis requires a large mass of precipitate (and so a large sample) and many time-consuming steps (filtering, drying to constant mass). (AAS is also specific to the element being analysed, and not affected by other substances that may co-precipitate.)

questions.question: A solution of oxalic acid ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4$), a weak diprotic acid, was prepared by dissolving 5.630 g in 250.0 mL of water. Calculate the concentration of the oxalic acid solution.

A solution of oxalic acid, a weak diprotic acid, is used to standardise a sodium hydroxide solution. With reference to TWO properties of oxalic acid, explain why it is suitable for use as a primary standard.
questions.answer: A primary standard must be available in a pure form, stable, and have an accurately known mass. Oxalic acid is chemically stable (it does not react with air or absorb water or carbon dioxide in significant amounts), so its concentration does not change over time, and it is a solid with a relatively high molar mass, so a reasonable mass can be weighed accurately on a balance with a small percentage uncertainty in the number of moles.

questions.question: A solution of oxalic acid of concentration 0.2501 mol L⁻¹ is used to standardise a sodium hydroxide solution. A number of 25.00 mL aliquots of the oxalic acid solution were titrated against the sodium hydroxide, with an average titre of 13.65 mL. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4(aq)+2\text{NaOH}(aq)\to\text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4(aq)+2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4)=0.2501\times0.02500=6.25\times10^{-3}$ mol. $n(\text{NaOH})=2\times6.25\times10^{-3}=1.25\times10^{-2}$ mol. $c(\text{NaOH})=\dfrac{1.25\times10^{-2}}{0.01365}=0.916$ mol L⁻¹.

questions.question: Compound W is but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. Reactions of W lead to compound Z (2-chlorobutane, CH3CHClCH2CH3) and to compound X, which is oxidised by acidified dichromate (H⁺/Cr₂O₇²⁻) to compound Y (butanone, CH3COCH2CH3). Name and draw the structural formula of compound X.
questions.answer: Compound X is butan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 (made by hydration of but-2-ene, with the OH group on carbon 2). It is a secondary alcohol, which is oxidised to the ketone butanone (Y).

questions.question: Compound W is but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. Reactions of W lead to compound Z (2-chlorobutane, CH3CHClCH2CH3) and to compound X, which is oxidised by acidified dichromate (H⁺/Cr₂O₇²⁻) to compound Y (butanone, CH3COCH2CH3). Identify the name of compound Z.
questions.answer: Compound Z is 2-chlorobutane (formed by the addition of HCl across the double bond of but-2-ene).

questions.question: Compound W is but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. Reactions of W lead to compound Z (2-chlorobutane, CH3CHClCH2CH3) and to compound X, which is oxidised by acidified dichromate (H⁺/Cr₂O₇²⁻) to compound Y (butanone, CH3COCH2CH3). Draw the reaction of compound W with bromine water, using structural formulae, and name the product formed.
questions.answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3+\text{Br}_2\to\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCHBrCH}_3$. The product is 2,3-dibromobutane (an addition reaction; the orange-brown bromine water is decolourised).

questions.question: A buffer solution has the property of resisting change in pH even when small amounts of acid or alkali are added to it. Using equilibrium principles, compare the change in pH of a 1:1 molar solution of $\text{CaCl}_{2}$/HCl and a 1:1 molar solution of $\text{NaH}_{2}\text{PO}_{4}$/$\text{Na}_{2}\text{HPO}_{4}$ when a small amount of acid is added to each mixture.
questions.answer: A buffer must contain a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) to react with added acid or base. $\text{CaCl}_{2}$/HCl is not a buffer: HCl is a strong acid which ionises completely, and its conjugate base $\text{Cl}^{-}$ is an extremely weak base which does not accept protons from water or from added acid. Calcium chloride is a neutral salt. There is nothing to remove added $\text{H}^{+}$, so the pH falls significantly when acid is added. $\text{NaH}_{2}\text{PO}_{4}$/$\text{Na}_{2}\text{HPO}_{4}$ is a buffer, containing the conjugate pair $\text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{4}^{-}$ (weak acid) and $\text{HPO}_{4}^{2-}$ (its conjugate base), in the equilibrium $\text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{4}^{-}$(aq) + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l) ⇌ $\text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$(aq) + $\text{HPO}_{4}^{2-}$(aq). When a small amount of acid is added, $\text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$ increases and, by Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts to the left: the added $\text{H}^{+}$ is consumed by the base $\text{HPO}_{4}^{2-}$ (forming $\text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{4}^{-}$), so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ and the pH change only slightly.

questions.question: Glucose is fermented by yeast according to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$(aq) → 2$\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$(aq) + 2$\text{CO}_{2}$(g). A student added 12 g of glucose to a conical flask along with 1 g of yeast and 50 mL of water at 37 °C. The flask was placed on a balance which monitored the mass of the reaction mixture over 24 hours (graph). Calculate the mass change in the conical flask by referring to the graph.
questions.answer: The mass falls from 128.68 g to 127.24 g, a mass change of 128.68 − 127.24 = 1.44 g (a loss, due to carbon dioxide escaping).

questions.question: Glucose (12 g) is fermented by yeast according to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$(aq) → 2$\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$(aq) + 2$\text{CO}_{2}$(g). The mass of the reaction mixture falls by 1.44 g (the graph shows a loss from 128.68 g to 127.24 g). Calculate the mass of ethanol produced by the reaction and compare this to a theoretical yield of ethanol. Show all working.
questions.answer: The mass lost is $\text{CO}_{2}$ (a gas which escapes). n($\text{CO}_{2}$) $=\dfrac{1.44}{44.01}=0.0327$ mol. The mole ratio $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$:$\text{CO}_{2}$ is 1:1, so n($\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$) = 0.0327 mol and m = 0.0327 × 46.07 = 1.5 g. Theoretical yield: n(glucose) $=\dfrac{12}{180.16}=0.0666$ mol; n($\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$) = 2 × 0.0666 = 0.133 mol; m = 0.133 × 46.07 = 6.1 g. The actual mass of ethanol (1.5 g) is lower than the theoretical yield (6.1 g), a percentage yield of about 25%.

questions.question: The white smoke reaction is a neutralisation reaction between the vapours of concentrated solutions of hydrochloric acid and ammonia. It is given its name due to the production of fine white salt crystals that are momentarily suspended in the air when the vapours react. Justify why this reaction can only be explained by the Brønsted-Lowry definition of acids and bases, and not the Arrhenius definition. Include a chemical equation in your answer.
questions.answer: HCl(g) + $\text{NH}_{3}$(g) → $\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl}$(s). The Arrhenius definition requires acids to release $\text{H}^{+}$ and bases to release $\text{OH}^{-}$ in aqueous solution, so it cannot be applied when the reaction occurs between gases (no water as a solvent), and ammonia has no hydroxide ion to release. The Brønsted-Lowry definition (acids are proton donors, and bases are proton acceptors) does not require water: HCl donates a proton to the lone pair on the $\text{NH}_{3}$ molecule, which accepts it, forming $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$, which form the white solid $\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl}$.

questions.question: The properties of three organic compounds Q, R and S are given: Q $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ (molecular weight 74.08, boiling point 141.2 °C, pKa 4.88); R $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ (73.14, 78 °C, pKa 10.21); S $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ (73.09, 213 °C). Name the three compounds tabulated above.
questions.answer: Q: propanoic acid. R: butan-1-amine. S: propanamide.

questions.question: Q is propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$, and R is butan-1-amine, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. Write TWO equations to compare the reactions that occur when compounds Q and R are individually added to water.
questions.answer: Propanoic acid is a weak acid: it donates a proton to water. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$(aq) + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l) ⇌ $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COO}^{-}$(aq) + $\text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$(aq). Butan-1-amine is a weak base: it accepts a proton from water. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$(l) + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l) ⇌ $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$(aq) + $\text{OH}^{-}$(aq).

questions.question: Three organic compounds have very similar molecular weights: propanoic acid ($\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$, boiling point 141.2 °C), butan-1-amine ($\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$, 78 °C) and propanamide ($\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$, 213 °C). Provide reasons for the variation in boiling points between the three compounds.
questions.answer: The boiling points depend on the strength of the intermolecular forces, since the molar masses (and so the dispersion forces) are similar. All three compounds can form hydrogen bonds. The amine (78 °C) has N–H bonds, which are the least polar of the three, since nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, and it has only one hydrogen-bonding group (–NH₂ with a lone pair), so it has the weakest hydrogen bonding and the lowest boiling point. The carboxylic acid (141 °C) has a highly polar O–H bond (oxygen is more electronegative) and a C=O group, so it forms stronger hydrogen bonds, including pairs of molecules (dimers), and has a higher boiling point. The amide (213 °C) has a polar C=O group and two N–H bonds that can each form hydrogen bonds, so it forms the most extensive hydrogen bonding network (more hydrogen bonds per molecule, with the highly polar amide group) and has the highest boiling point.

questions.question: Four 0.1 M solutions of silver nitrate, lead nitrate, iron(III) nitrate and potassium nitrate are contained in separate, unlabelled bottles. Describe a series of laboratory tests that would successfully identify these solutions. Where appropriate, provide supporting chemical equations and predicted observations.
questions.answer: (Marking criteria only were given by the school; this is a sample answer.) Test 1 – colour: the $\text{Fe(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{3}$ solution is yellow-brown, while the others are colourless. Test 2 – add dilute sodium hydroxide solution to a sample of each. $\text{Fe(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{3}$: a red-brown precipitate forms: $\text{Fe}^{3+}$(aq) + 3$\text{OH}^{-}$(aq) → $\text{Fe(OH)}_{3}$(s). $\text{AgNO}_{3}$: a brown (grey-brown) precipitate of silver oxide forms: 2$\text{Ag}^{+}$(aq) + 2$\text{OH}^{-}$(aq) → $\text{Ag}_{2}\text{O}$(s) + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$(l). $\text{Pb(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$: a white precipitate forms: $\text{Pb}^{2+}$(aq) + 2$\text{OH}^{-}$(aq) → $\text{Pb(OH)}_{2}$(s), which dissolves in excess NaOH (amphoteric). $\text{KNO}_{3}$: no precipitate (all potassium salts and nitrates are soluble); the potassium can be confirmed by a lilac flame test. Confirmation: adding dilute sodium chloride gives a white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$ with the silver nitrate: $\text{Ag}^{+}$(aq) + $\text{Cl}^{-}$(aq) → $\text{AgCl}$(s).

questions.question: A conductivity titration was performed to determine the concentration of a hydrochloric acid solution. A 25.0 mL sample of the acid was placed into a conductivity cell. A burette was used to slowly dispense volumes of 0.500 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide. Conductivity readings (S cm⁻¹) for volumes of 0, 1.0, 2.0, … 10.0 mL of NaOH were 3.4, 3.1, 2.6, 2.1, 1.8, 1.4, 1.1, 1.6, 1.8, 2.3 and 2.7 respectively. Graph the data in the table using intersecting lines of best fit and perform relevant calculations to determine the concentration of the hydrochloric acid solution.
questions.answer: Plot conductivity (vertical axis, S cm⁻¹) against volume of NaOH added (horizontal axis, mL) and draw two lines of best fit: a falling line for 0–6 mL, since the highly conductive $\text{H}^{+}$ ions are replaced by less conductive $\text{Na}^{+}$ ions as the acid is neutralised, and a rising line for 7–10 mL, as excess $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions are added. The lines intersect at the equivalence point, at about 6.0 mL. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. n(NaOH) = 0.500 × 0.0060 = 3.0 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl). $c_{\text{HCl}}$ = 3.0 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.12 mol L⁻¹.

questions.question: Compare the structures, properties and uses of TWO named addition polymers.
questions.answer: (Marking criteria only were given by the school; this is a sample answer comparing low-density polyethylene (LDPE) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC).) Structure: both are addition polymers formed from monomers containing a C=C double bond, which opens up to form a chain of single bonds. LDPE is made from ethene, giving –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ– with a non-polar chain, which is highly branched, so the chains cannot pack closely together. PVC is made from chloroethene, giving –(CH₂–CHCl)ₙ–, in which the polar C–Cl bond gives stronger dipole–dipole forces between the chains. Properties: LDPE has only weak dispersion forces between the chains, so it is soft, flexible, has a low density and a low melting point, and is chemically unreactive and waterproof. PVC has stronger intermolecular forces (dipole–dipole as well as dispersion), so it is harder and more rigid and has a higher softening temperature (it can be made flexible by adding plasticisers). Uses: LDPE is used for plastic bags, cling wrap, squeeze bottles and food packaging, because it is flexible. PVC is used for pipes, window frames and electrical insulation (rigid PVC) and for flooring and hoses (plasticised PVC), taking advantage of its strength and durability.

questions.question: A 40.0 mL solution of $2.00\times10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹ sodium sulfate is added to 200 mL of $2.00\times10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹ lead(II) nitrate. Perform calculations to determine whether a precipitate of lead(II) sulfate will form.
questions.answer: $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)+\text{Pb(NO}_3)_2(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{PbSO}_4(s)+2\text{NaNO}_3(aq)$. $n(\text{SO}_4^{2-})=0.0400\times2.00\times10^{-3}=8.0\times10^{-5}$ mol. $n(\text{Pb}^{2+})=0.200\times2.00\times10^{-3}=4.0\times10^{-4}$ mol. Total volume $=240$ mL $=0.240$ L. $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=\dfrac{8.0\times10^{-5}}{0.240}=3.33\times10^{-4}$ M. $[\text{Pb}^{2+}]=\dfrac{4.0\times10^{-4}}{0.240}=1.67\times10^{-3}$ M. $Q=[\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=(1.67\times10^{-3})(3.33\times10^{-4})=5.56\times10^{-7}$. $K_{sp}(\text{PbSO}_4)=2.53\times10^{-8}$ (data sheet). Since $Q>K_{sp}$, a precipitate of lead(II) sulfate will form.
